meta.title: Who really said "Once you have tasted flight, you will forever walk the earth with your eyes turned skyward, for there you have been and there you will always long to return"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — Leonardo da Vinci never wrote this. It was written by John H. Secondari for the 1965 ABC film “I, Leonardo da Vinci,” then mis-credited to Leonardo.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Once you have tasted flight, you will forever walk the earth with your eyes turned skyward, for there you have been and there you will always long to return'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Leonardo. Screenwriter John H. Secondari wrote it to voice Leonardo’s thoughts in a 1965 documentary; the exact popular wording is a later paraphrase.

answer.label: Not Leonardo da Vinci — written by John H. Secondari
answer.authorDates: 1919–1975 · American author, journalist & TV documentary producer
answer.sourceLine: This line was written by John H. Secondari to voice Leonardo’s imagined thoughts in the 1965 ABC documentary I, Leonardo da Vinci (from the series The Saga of Western Man). It appears nowhere in Leonardo’s own notebooks or letters. The film’s wording was “And once you have tasted flight you will walk the earth with your eyes turned skyward; for there you have been, and there you would return” — the now-famous version (“forever” … “always long to return”) is a later paraphrase that spread after 1975.

source.excerpt: And once you have tasted flight you will walk the earth with your eyes turned skyward; for there you have been, and there you would return.
trail: Quote Investigator concludes the line “was created by John H. Secondari” for the 1965 film I, Leonardo da Vinci, and that researchers found nothing like it in Leonardo’s writings.
The film’s line read “…there you have been, and there you would return”; a 1975 Analog epigraph by George R. R. Martin and Lisa Tuttle shifted it toward “there you long to return,” per QI.
By the mid-1970s the reworded line was being “incorrectly reassigned directly to Leonardo” in aviation and skydiving coverage, as noted by Air Facts Journal.
source.excerptNote: The wording as written by John H. Secondari for the 1965 film. The widely-shared “forever … always long to return” version is a later alteration, not Leonardo’s and not the film’s exact line.

author.name: John H. Secondari
author.heading: About John H. Secondari
author.metaLine: 1919–1975 · American author, journalist & TV documentary producer
author.bio: John Hermes Secondari was an American novelist, foreign correspondent, and television producer who created and wrote ABC’s acclaimed documentary series The Saga of Western Man. Working with his wife and co-producer Helen Jean Rogers, he earned multiple Emmy and Peabody awards for historical films. For the 1965 episode I, Leonardo da Vinci, he scripted first-person passages voicing Leonardo’s thoughts — including the “tasted flight” line later mistaken for Leonardo’s own words.

misattribution.heading: How it became a “Leonardo” quote
misattribution.intro: One of the internet’s most-shared “Leonardo da Vinci” lines was never written by Leonardo. It was scripted for him in a 1960s television documentary, then drifted loose from its source.

items.why: No such passage appears in Leonardo’s notebooks or letters. Quote Investigator reports researchers could not locate it anywhere in his writings; the attribution is a 20th-century error.
Secondari wrote the line to voice Leonardo’s imagined thoughts in the 1965 ABC film I, Leonardo da Vinci, per QI. The film’s wording was “…there you have been, and there you would return.”

items.who: George R. R. Martin & Lisa Tuttle (1975)
items.why: A 1975 Analog story used the line as an epigraph in a slightly altered form; from there the reworded version (“forever” … “long to return”) spread through skydiving and aviation writing under Leonardo’s name, as traced by QI.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentiment fits Leonardo’s real fascination with flight, but the words are John H. Secondari’s — written in 1965, not the Renaissance — per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why the mix-up stuck
lead: Leonardo genuinely studied birds and designed flying machines, so a soaring line about flight feels authentically his. That plausibility is exactly what let a scriptwriter’s words pass for the master’s.

Secondari’s documentary put the sentence in Leonardo’s mouth as dramatized narration. Audiences and later quoters dropped the framing, and the line was repeated as though quoted from Leonardo’s own notebooks.
context.detailsSummary: The path from film script to “Leonardo quote”
detailsBody: 1965: John H. Secondari scripts the line for I, Leonardo da Vinci as first-person narration.
1975: a slightly reworded form appears as an epigraph in a George R. R. Martin & Lisa Tuttle story in Analog, and the line begins to be credited directly to Leonardo.
Late 1970s onward: skydiving, hang-gliding, and aviation writing spread the reworded “forever … always long to return” version under Leonardo’s name.
context.pull: The thought suits Leonardo. The words are a 1965 screenwriter’s.
